chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Legal, Regulatory and Tax Basics in India

lessons.title: Angel Tax, Capital Gains and FEMA: What Indian Angels Must Know

children.text: For more than a decade, Indian founders dreaded two words: angel tax. Raise money at a premium the tax department disagreed with, and the startup could be taxed on its own investors' cheques. That rule is now gone. What has not gone away is tax on your gains when you exit, the rules on using your losses, and FEMA, the foreign exchange law that applies the moment money crosses a border. And from 1 April 2026, a new Income-tax Act has replaced the 1961 law. This lesson gives you the working knowledge every Indian angel needs, and tells you exactly when to call a chartered accountant.

body.text: Tax rarely decides whether an angel investment works, but getting it wrong can quietly take a large slice of a rare winner. Track three things for every deal: how long you have held it, whether the shares are listed when you sell, and whose money, resident or non-resident, went in.

children.text: Angel Tax: The Rule That Is Gone

markDefs.definition: The former Section 56(2)(viib) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, which taxed an unlisted company on share premium received above the shares' fair market value, treating the excess as the company's income.

children.text: Angel tax

was introduced to stop unaccounted money being routed into companies disguised as inflated share premium. In practice, it also caught genuine startups whose valuations were based on future potential rather than current assets. The tax fell on the company, not the investor, but it made founders nervous about every angel round.

body.title: The rise and fall of angel tax

events.title: Introduced
events.description: The Finance Act, 2012 adds Section 56(2)(viib), taxing share premium above fair market value received from resident investors.

events.title: Extended to non-residents
events.description: The Finance Act, 2023 removes the residency condition, so premium from foreign investors is also covered.

events.title: Abolition announced
events.description: The Union Budget proposes scrapping the provision entirely for all classes of investors.

events.title: Abolished
events.description: The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 makes the provision inapplicable, removing angel tax for resident and non-resident investors alike.

body.text: Gone does not mean irrelevant. Pending assessments for earlier years can still be pursued under the old provision. Valuation also still matters elsewhere: FEMA sets pricing rules for shares issued to non-residents, and a separate income-tax rule can tax a person who receives shares for less than their fair market value. A genuine, well-documented valuation report remains good practice in every round.

children.text: Capital Gains When You Sell

markDefs.definition: Securities Transaction Tax: a small tax charged on trades in listed securities on Indian stock exchanges. Paying it is a condition for the concessional equity tax rates.

children.text: The biggest tax question at exit is whether your shares are unlisted or listed at the time of sale. Most angel exits, including acquisitions and secondary sales, involve unlisted shares. Selling on NSE or BSE after an IPO, with
STT

paid, brings you under the listed equity rules. You do not lose the listed rate just because you bought the shares before listing without paying STT: a CBDT notification of October 2018 relaxes the STT-on-acquisition condition for shares acquired while unlisted, and your holding period counts from the date you originally acquired them.

body.caption: Capital gains tax on shares for individuals (rates before surcharge and cess)

cells: Unlisted shares (most acquisitions and secondary sales)
Listed equity shares sold with STT paid (for example, after an IPO)
12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh in a year

body.title: What changed with the Income-tax Act, 2025?

children.text: The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaced the Income-tax Act, 1961 from 1 April 2026. The most visible change is terminology: "previous year" and "assessment year" are replaced by a single "tax year" running from 1 April to 31 March. The capital gains rates and holding periods in the table continue, but section numbers have changed. Many articles and older documents still cite 1961 sections such as 112A, so check which law a source is referring to, especially for sales straddling April 2026.
Worked example: Meghna invested ₹10 lakh in unlisted shares of a Pune SaaS startup. Five years later, the company is acquired and she receives ₹60 lakh in cash.

body.caption: Held more than 24 months, so the gain is long-term. Meghna keeps ₹53.75 lakh before surcharge and cess.

body.title: The cost of selling early
body.prompt: Suppose Meghna's company is acquired after only 20 months instead, for the same ₹60 lakh on her ₹10 lakh cost. Her slab rate is 30%. Ignoring surcharge and cess, how much tax does she pay, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: 20 months is not more than 24 months, so the ₹50 lakh gain is short-term and taxed at her slab rate: ₹50 lakh × 30% = ₹15 lakh. That is ₹8.75 lakh more than the long-term tax of ₹6.25 lakh. When a secondary sale is optional, the timing relative to the 24-month mark can matter a lot.

body.text: Acquisitions with escrow, earn-outs or payment in the buyer's shares can create tax questions that do not match your cash flow, including on amounts you have not yet received or on shares you cannot sell. Before signing any exit documents, ask a chartered accountant how each component will be taxed and when.

children.text: Using Your Losses

Since most angel investments fail, loss rules matter as much as gain rules. A capital loss generally arises when there is a transfer, such as selling shares for a nominal price or receiving a final distribution when a company is wound up. Simply holding shares in a dead company may not, on its own, give you a loss you can use. The main set-off rules:
Short-term capital losses
can be set off against both short-term and long-term capital gains.
Long-term capital losses
can be set off only against long-term capital gains.
Unused capital losses

can be carried forward for up to 8 years, but only if you file your return by the due date. Valid capital losses from before 1 April 2026 carry into the Income-tax Act, 2025 with their original character, and are set off in the same way the 1961 Act allowed, so older long-term losses still offset only long-term gains.

body.caption: How losses reduce tax on a winner (illustrative, all long-term, before surcharge and cess)

cells: Long-term losses from five failed startups, formally transferred

body.label: Converting CCPS or notes into equity
body.context: Converting preference shares of a company into its equity shares is not treated as a transfer, so no capital gains tax arises at conversion. The equity shares inherit the cost of the preference shares, and the holding period includes the time you held the preference shares. Convertible notes can be treated differently, so check those with your chartered accountant.

body.title: Where can the loss go?
body.question: In tax year 2026-27, Rahul makes a ₹12 lakh long-term capital loss from a failed startup and a ₹20 lakh short-term capital gain from selling other shares. What can he do with the loss?
options: Set it off against the ₹20 lakh short-term gain
Set it off against his salary income
He cannot use it this year, but can carry it forward for up to 8 years to set off against future long-term gains, if he files his return on time
Nothing; startup losses can never be used
body.explanation: A long-term capital loss can be set off only against long-term capital gains. With no long-term gains this year, Rahul should carry it forward, which requires filing his return by the due date. Capital losses can never be set off against salary.

children.text: FEMA: When Money Crosses Borders

markDefs.definition: An investment by a non-resident where the original capital and returns can be freely sent back abroad, subject to taxes and reporting.
The part of India's non-debt instrument rules under which NRIs and OCIs invest on a non-repatriation basis; such investment is treated like a domestic investment.

children.text: The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 governs two situations angels meet often: an NRI investing in an Indian startup, and a resident Indian investing in a startup based abroad. For NRIs, the key choice is between a
repatriation basis
and a non-repatriation basis under
Schedule IV

body.caption: How an NRI can invest in an unlisted Indian startup

cells: NRE or FCNR(B) account, or inward remittance
Issue price cannot be below fair value under an internationally accepted pricing methodology, duly certified; valuation not older than 90 days
Treated as domestic investment; FDI pricing rules generally do not apply
Form FC-GPR within 30 days of allotment
Sale proceeds can be repatriated abroad after tax
Proceeds go to the NRO account; remittance abroad is subject to NRO limits, generally up to $1 million a financial year after tax

children.text: The reverse case is increasingly common. Many Indian founders incorporate a parent company in Delaware or Singapore. If you are a resident Indian investing in such a company, you are sending money abroad under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme, which allows up to $250,000 per person per financial year. An investment in an unlisted foreign company is treated as overseas direct investment under the Overseas Investment Rules, 2022, not portfolio investment. Resident individuals can make such investments only in an operating foreign company that is not engaged in financial services, and cannot invest this way in a company they control if it has subsidiaries or step-down subsidiaries. The remittance and reporting run through your bank.

body.title: NRI investing into India vs resident investing abroad

columns.label: NRI into an Indian startup
points: Choose repatriation (NRE or FCNR) or non-repatriation (NRO) at the start
Repatriable investment must meet fair value pricing rules
The Indian company files FC-GPR within 30 days
Indian capital gains tax applies on exit, and TDS may be deducted

columns.label: Resident into a foreign startup
points: Money goes out under LRS, up to $250,000 per person per financial year
Unlisted foreign shares count as overseas direct investment
The company must be an operating business, not engaged in financial services
You must report the foreign asset in your Indian tax return

body.title: Riya's route
body.question: Riya is an NRI in Dubai. She wants to invest ₹15 lakh in a Mumbai startup and expects to move any sale proceeds back to Dubai. Which route fits best?
options: Non-repatriation basis through her NRO account
Repatriation basis through her NRE account, with the company following FDI pricing and FC-GPR reporting
Ask a resident friend to invest on her behalf
body.explanation: Since Riya wants the money to go back abroad freely, a repatriation-basis investment through her NRE account fits. The company must issue shares at or above certified fair value and file FC-GPR within 30 days. Investing through a resident nominee to avoid FEMA rules is not a legitimate route, and LRS is for residents sending money out of India.

body.title: Arvind's tax year
body.scenario:
Arvind, a Chennai-based angel, has a busy year.
1. One portfolio company is acquired for cash. He held it for 3 years and makes a ₹40 lakh gain.
2. Two other startups he held for 4 years were wound up, giving him a combined long-term capital loss of ₹12 lakh.
3. He wants to put $50,000 into a Singapore-incorporated startup founded by two IIT Madras graduates.
4. His brother, an NRI in California, wants to invest ₹20 lakh alongside him in an Indian startup and may later move the money back to the US.
body.prompt: Walk through the tax and FEMA points Arvind should raise with his chartered accountant.
body.modelAnswer:
1. The acquisition gain is long-term, as unlisted shares were held for more than 24 months. At 12.5%, tax on ₹40 lakh would be ₹5 lakh before surcharge and cess.
2. If the ₹12 lakh loss is an allowable long-term capital loss in the same tax year, it can be set off: ₹40 lakh − ₹12 lakh = ₹28 lakh taxable, and tax falls to ₹3.5 lakh. He should confirm the wind-ups count as transfers and keep the documents.
3. He must file his return by the due date so that any unused losses can be carried forward.
4. The Singapore investment goes out under LRS, within his $250,000 annual limit. As an unlisted foreign company, it is overseas direct investment under the 2022 rules: the company must run a bona fide business, not be a restricted financial services entity, and the remittance and reporting run through his bank. He must also disclose the foreign asset in his tax return.
5. His brother should invest on a repatriation basis through an NRE account if he wants to move the money back to the US. The Indian company must issue shares at or above certified fair value and file FC-GPR within 30 days. Tax on his eventual gain will be governed by Indian law and the India-US tax treaty, with TDS likely on sale.

body.title: The holding period
body.textWithBlank: Gains on unlisted shares are long-term only if the shares are held for more than ___ months.
body.explanation: Unlisted shares need more than 24 months to qualify as long-term, taxed at 12.5% without indexation. Listed equity shares sold with STT need only more than 12 months.

cards.definition: The former tax on share premium above fair market value, abolished from AY 2025-26 by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024.
Held more than 24 months; taxed at 12.5% without indexation.
Held more than 12 months with STT paid; 12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year.
Can be set off only against long-term gains; carry forward up to 8 years if the return is filed on time.
The single 1 April to 31 March period used by the Income-tax Act, 2025 from 1 April 2026.
NRI investment through NRE or FCNR accounts, following FDI pricing rules, with proceeds freely repatriable.
NRI or OCI investment on a non-repatriation basis through an NRO account, treated like domestic investment.
Liberalised Remittance Scheme: lets a resident individual send up to $250,000 abroad per financial year.

points: Angel tax on share premium was abolished for all investors from AY 2025-26, but valuation still matters for FEMA and other tax rules.
Unlisted shares held more than 24 months are taxed at 12.5% without indexation; shorter holdings are taxed at slab rates.
Listed shares sold with STT after more than 12 months are taxed at 12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year; short-term gains at 20%.
Long-term capital losses can offset only long-term gains, and carrying losses forward requires filing your return on time.
NRIs choose repatriation (NRE or FCNR, FDI pricing, FC-GPR) or non-repatriation (NRO, Schedule IV) at the start.
Residents investing in foreign startups use LRS, up to $250,000 a year, and unlisted foreign shares count as overseas direct investment.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax, legal or investment advice. Tax and FEMA rules are detailed, depend on your residential status and circumstances, and change frequently, including with the transition to the Income-tax Act, 2025. Rates shown exclude surcharge and cess. All people and figures are illustrative. Consult a qualified chartered accountant and legal professional before investing or exiting.
